items.why: The command clearly distinguishes taking the woman out from killing anyone who follows her.
The threat to David and Abishai’s rescue clearly identify the slain Philistine as Ishbi-Benob.
The request and its fulfillment clearly identify the man of God as the one praying.
The officer’s skeptical question clearly anchors Elisha’s warning that he will see but not eat the food.
Their admission leads directly to a clear new plan: report the good news to the palace.
It mainly tests the presentation order of two killings in separate battles, while 'kills first' sounds like a contest.
The key omits what God forbade, so it does not fully explain the refusal.
God’s help is explicitly tied to three groups, though answering mostly requires reproducing the list.
The answer simply repeats the opening statement that Jeroboam did not change his evil ways.
Both the reference to following 'him' and the priests’ direct address identify Uzziah.
Uzziah is clearly Amaziah’s son, and making him king supplies an unambiguous purpose.
Reading the letter heading distinguishes its sender, Claudius Lysias, from its recipient.
The speaker’s 'my son' and the other woman’s hidden son clearly establish whose child was eaten.
The city is stated before the tomb, making this mostly a straightforward sequence check.
Talking until daylight is the last narrated activity before Paul leaves.
The wording clearly distinguishes the two officers receiving orders from the troops they must prepare.
The sequence is clear, but the question presents the king’s account of enemy intentions without acknowledging its source.
The contrast between the soldiers returning and the cavalry continuing makes the reference clear.
Both illnesses and evil spirits stop afflicting people, so ordinary wording about what 'leaves' does not uniquely select the key.
The order tells all five companies to guard the temple; the key incorrectly singles out only the two going off duty.
The final 'he' clearly refers to Uzziah and explains why he has his fields worked.
The final summary credits David and his men collectively, rather than Jonathan alone.
Consent and Paul’s transfer can both be understood as prerequisites, so 'must happen before' does not isolate the key.
The passage explicitly links Paul’s long speech to his planned departure the next day.
Tracking the nested quotation identifies the other woman’s own son as the child planned for tomorrow.
The king’s command and the direction of his outstretched hand identify the man of God.
The messengers’ return and report directly precede the people going to plunder.
Elisha calls the sender a murderer, and the excerpt identifies the king as that sender.
Uzziah’s eagerness is explicitly linked to his affliction, not merely to the priests hurrying him out.
Mobilizing comes first in a single sentence, so the task offers little beyond locating the first action.
The question meaningfully paraphrases Zechariah’s instruction in the fear of God as teaching reverence.
'Assembling materials' is an unnatural, vague substitute for bringing their scrolls together.
The officer’s appointment at the gate makes the following 'him' readily identifiable.
The warning clearly addresses the man from Judah, though 'whose body is warned' is awkward wording.
The answer is explicit, but 'the addressee' adds unnecessary letter-analysis terminology for ordinary readers.
The passage distinguishes Jehoiada, who hands over the weapons, from David, who once owned them.
Athaliah goes after hearing the crowd; seeing the king happens only after she arrives.
The text explicitly makes Athaliah’s death the reason for the city’s calm.
'Under their command' points to the family leaders, not the officials who counted the troops.
The father requests the donkey and the sons saddle it for him, clearly establishing who rides.
'The news' merely repeats the sentence without specifying the report that the camp was deserted.
The victims of the possessed man’s beating are clearly the seven sons, resolving the final 'they'.
The Arameans distinguish Israel’s king, who supposedly hired help, from the Hittite and Egyptian attackers.
The departing 'he' follows a sentence involving both men, leaving the lion’s victim insufficiently secure in this excerpt.
The fulfilled warning links the later 'him' to the officer addressed as 'you'.
Paul identifies the young man as the messenger, and the centurion repeats that identification.
The claimed invitation is to bring the man of God back so that he can eat and drink.
The last sentence supplies the answer directly, making this mostly a narrative-order check.
The future 'he' refers to the promised son Josiah, not Jeroboam standing at the altar.
The conspirators want the council to request the transfer and the commander to carry it out.
'Who gives the message that he says will happen' awkwardly blurs the original messenger and the current speaker.
'Ahaziah’s son’s nurse' adds a needless relationship chain to an otherwise simple identification.
The men distinguish their rejected options from their clear decision to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The first covenant includes the Lord as well as the king and people, unlike the second.
